transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-26
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE); Samir Desai (Redwood SE); Ivy Chen (Redwood CSM); Anita Gomez (Rivermark Head of Platform); Mark Li (Rivermark SRE); Priya Shah (Rivermark ML Eng); Raj Patel (Rivermark Security)

Summary:
- Weekly POC sync focused on latency tuning: TTFT, streaming, sequence length profiles, and kernel choices. Reviewed benchmark numbers from last week's run and decided next steps for tuning and validation.

Topics:
- TTFT (time-to-first-token) regressions on hosted vs dedicated
- Streaming improvements & partial token emission
- Sequence length distribution impact (avg 280, p95 ~ 640)
- Kernel selection tradeoffs (FP16 vs int8 quantized kernels)
- Data residency and security checklist items

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, um, this is the weekly latency tuning sync for the Rivermark POC. Samir has the bench notes.
[00:18] Samir Desai: Hi all, yeah, quick agenda, review TTFT numbers from the last run, look at streaming latency improvements we tried, and then dive into kernel mapping changes I pushed to the test cluster.
[00:32] Anita Gomez: Sounds good. We saw a couple of outliers last week, TTFT spikes around 220ms to 400ms which were higher than we expected. Curious what's causing them.
[00:45] Mark Li: yep, we also saw p95 token latency jump during traffic bursts. Our production target is 150ms TTFT and p95 <= 300ms for single-request flows.
[01:05] Samir Desai: Right, quick recap: last week we ran on the dedicated pool with the Redwood-verified 13B model quantized to int8 and used the fast-attn kernel. Average TTFT for cold requests was around 120ms but warm was 70ms; the spikes Anita mentions correlate with first-in-batch requests when cache miss happens.
[01:32] Priya Shah: can you clarify 'first-in-batch' correlation? is that because KV cache isn't primed?
[01:40] Samir Desai: Exactly—if prefix caching isn't used or if the request hits a new seq-length path kernel, the runtime has to select and JIT the kernel, and that adds overhead. We also saw a couple of kernel fallbacks to a more general path which cost ~80ms.
[02:05] Raj Patel: quick sec—on security—does any of the caching persist to disk or shared across tenants? We need assurance it's in-GPU RAM only.
[02:14] Samir Desai: Good question: for the dedicated pool we're using per-tenant KV cache in GPU memory only, not persisted to disk; configs are in the sandbox and we can enable stricter isolation.
[02:30] Lena Park: ok, going to the numbers spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.infer/bench/rvk-2028-07-20) — Samir, walk us through TTFT table.
[02:45] Samir Desai: Sure, so column A is cold TTFT, column B warm, C is p95 per experiment. Experiment 1 used default kernel mapping, Experiment 2 forced fast-attn for seq <= 512, Experiment 3 used streaming with eager partial emit. For seq avg=280, Experiment 2 shaved about 18% off overall TTFT, but for p95 long tails we saw improvements only when we primed cache.
[03:12] Anita Gomez: priming cache — operationally how would we do that? Our callers are often stateless; we can't rely on warm cache.
[03:22] Samir Desai: There are a couple options: 1) prefetch commonly used prefixes at model load, 2) use a short-lived warm-up probe for new pods during scale-up, or 3) accept slightly higher cold TTFT but optimize kernel selection to reduce JIT time. Prefetch is the most predictable but adds a small steady cost.
[03:44] Priya Shah: What about streaming? We saw partial token emission reduced perceived latency in our front-end tests. Did you enable eager streaming in Experiment 3?
[03:56] Samir Desai: Yes, Experiment 3 toggled streaming.emit_early = true. That reduced time-to-first-byte in the client by ~60ms on avg for mid-length sequences, but when combined with quantized kernels we saw some jitter because the streaming path used a different kernel set leading to occasional fallbacks.
[04:22] Mark Li: Those fallbacks—are they predictable? We need deterministic latency.
[04:29] Samir Desai: Mostly predictable; they trigger when sequence length crosses the precompiled kernel boundary or when memory pressure forces a generic kernel. I added a conservative kernel map that favors precompiled kernels for the p50-p95 bucket to avoid jitter.
[04:47] Anita Gomez: Any impact to throughput if we bias kernels that way?
[04:52] Samir Desai: Slightly; throughput drops ~5-8% on sustained batch workloads if you lock kernels, but single-request latency improves. That's the cost/latency tradeoff we discussed.
[05:06] Lena Park: quick check—what hardware were these runs on?
[05:10] Samir Desai: Dedicated A100s for the main runs; we also ran a subset on an H100 dev node to validate kernel differences. The H100 runs showed better int8 path performance, TTFT improved ~12% vs A100 for the same config, but cost per GPU hour is higher.
[05:30] Raj Patel: From compliance side, confirm: any model artifacts or KV cache ever leave the customer's VPC?
[05:36] Ivy Chen: For Private deployments yes, everything stays in-customer VPC; for Dedicated it's isolated but controlled by Redwood infra; we can provide SOC2 attestations. We'll follow up with the security packet.
[05:52] Priya Shah: Samir, can you explain kernel selection logic again? We saw terms like 'fast-attn', 'general', and 'low-memory'.
[06:03] Samir Desai: Sure—fast-attn is optimized for common transformer patterns and short-to-medium seqs, general is a fallback that handles all shapes but is slower, low-memory uses a streaming-friendly kernel with lower peak memory at some latency cost. The runtime chooses based on sequence length, kv-cache presence, and available memory headroom.
[06:28] Mark Li: For our workload distribution (avg 280, p95 640), what's your recommendation?
[06:36] Samir Desai: For that profile, conservative mapping: use fast-attn up to 512, use low-memory for 513-1024 when concurrency is high, and avoid forcing general unless necessary. Also enable streaming.emit_early for finishes under 800 tokens; that improves perceived latency.
[06:57] Priya Shah: Any quantization caveats? We saw a small quality delta with int8 for a couple of prompts.
[07:06] Samir Desai: Yes, int8 can introduce slight quality regressions on rare prompts, recommended flow is int8 for non-critical paths and keep fp16 for critical endpoints or run regression checks on prompt set. Redwood Optimize suggested a hybrid: int8 for background batched endpoints, fp16 for real-time customer-facing flows.
[07:28] Anita Gomez: Do you have automated regression checks integrated so we can flag quality drop during kernel switches?
[07:34] Samir Desai: We do—our quality monitor ties to prompt sets and flags drift; we can add a regression alert for any change >X perplexity or human-specified metrics. We'll enable that for the pilot.
[07:50] Lena Park: Ok, concrete items: Samir you mentioned a tuned runtime config. Where will you drop that?
[07:58] Samir Desai: I'll push to the shared S3 / test config bucket: s3://redwood-poc/rivermark/kernel-maps/2028-07-26 and post the link in the CRM note. It includes a 'conservative' and an 'aggressive' mapping and a script to toggle prefetching.
[08:16] Priya Shah: We'll run the conservative mapping this week and report back. Also I'll run the microbench focusing on seq lengths 64/256/512/768 and attach the logs.
[08:27] Mark Li: For the TTFT spike correlation you mentioned earlier—do you have traces that show JIT overhead?
[08:34] Samir Desai: Yes, we collected tracing data; there's a JIT compile marker that aligns with a ~60-90ms bump. I've annotated the bench spreadsheet and included sample flamegraphs.
[08:48] Raj Patel: On compliance doc delivery—what do you need from us to expedite?
[08:53] Ivy Chen: We'll send the SOC2 and ISO docs and a short questionnaire; Raj, can you share any specific local residency requirements?
[08:59] Raj Patel: We need data residency in the EU for a subset of customers; it's on the checklist.
[09:06] Lena Park: Noted. We'll mark that as a constraint for routing and dedicated regions.
[09:12] Anita Gomez: question—cost delta if we run H100 vs A100 for the low-latency path?
[09:19] Samir Desai: Ballpark H100 is ~25-35% more per GPU hour but gives ~10-15% TTFT improvement in our runs. For small clusters the cost delta can be worth it if it reduces instance count. We'll include a cost model with Lena's pricing note.
[09:38] Priya Shah: small note—we saw a weird case where streaming with int8 produced partial tokens that were slightly garbled at the boundary; might be a decoder quant rounding artifact. We can reproduce and attach examples.
[09:50] Samir Desai: good catch. We'll add a regression test for streaming+int8 to the quality suite.
[09:58] Lena Park: ok, recap of next steps out loud: Samir to post tuned configs + kernel map link by Friday, Priya to run focused microbench and attach logs, Raj to confirm residency/compliance asks, Lena to send pricing and contract template. Any objections?
[10:15] Anita Gomez: none. Sounds good.
[10:20] Mark Li: We'll also schedule a short live run during our spike window next Tuesday to validate p95 under load.
[10:28] Lena Park: Great—I'll book that. Thanks everyone.
[10:34] Meeting end.
